issues.legal_issue: A transfer of granted land after the grant's non-alienation period still requires prior government permission when the transfer occurs after the statutory prohibition has commenced.
material_facts: The lands were granted to members of protected communities subject to a fifteen-year non-alienation condition.
The transfers were made after that period had expired, but no valid prior permission from the competent authority had been obtained.
Documents presented as evidence of permission were found by the authorities to be forged and fabricated.
The purchaser argued that permission was unnecessary once the grant's fifteen-year restriction had expired.
issues.conclusion: Prior permission remained necessary after the grant's non-alienation period expired. Because valid prior permission had not been obtained, the transfers were void and the orders nullifying them were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 4(2) of the Karnataka Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prohibition of Transfer of Certain Lands) Act, 1978 make a transfer in breach of the statutory requirement of previous government permission void. Section 11 gives the Act overriding effect. Rule 9 of the Karnataka Land Grant Rules, 1969 does not displace that statutory requirement. Dharma Naika v. Rama Naika explains that a post-commencement transfer without prior permission is void; Harishchandra Hegde v. State of Karnataka recognizes the overriding effect of the Act. Manchegowda v. State of Karnataka concerned a limited challenge to the Act and does not establish that post-restriction transfers need no permission.

predicates.granted_land_transfer: A grantee transferred land that had been granted subject to restrictions.
predicates.statutory_transfer_prohibition_in_force: The transfer occurred while a statutory prohibition on transferring granted land without prior government permission applied.
predicates.no_valid_prior_permission: The grantee and transferee completed the transfer without obtaining valid prior permission from the government.

issues.definition: When granted land is transferred while the statutory permission requirement applies and no valid prior permission was obtained, the transfer is void.

issues.legal_issue: A delay of approximately eight years in seeking restoration does not by itself bar action to nullify an unauthorized transfer of granted land under a beneficial protective law.
material_facts: The transfers occurred in 1997 and villagers sought action against them in 2005.
The authority acted under legislation intended to protect members of protected communities from exploitation involving granted land.
The court found that the delay was not comparable to the substantially longer delays considered in the cases cited by the purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The delay of approximately eight years was not sufficient to invalidate the authority's action; the restoration proceedings were not barred by delay.
issues.legal_principle: Where no limitation period is prescribed, action must be taken within a reasonable time, assessed in light of the circumstances and statutory purpose. Ibrahimpatnam Taluk Vyavasaya Coolie Sangham v. K. Suresh Reddy, Situ Sahu v. State of Jharkhand, Chhedi Lal Yadav v. Hari Kishore Yadav, and Vivek M. Hinduja address reasonable time in exercising statutory powers. Amrendra Pratap Singh v. Tej Bahadur Prajapati supports the conclusion that limitation principles do not defeat protective action concerning tribal property. In this case, an eight-year delay in a proceeding under beneficial protective legislation was not unreasonable enough to bar action.

rule.if: granted_land_restoration_proceeding and unauthorized_transfer and authority_acted_after_moderate_delay and protective_statutory_purpose

predicates.granted_land_restoration_proceeding: An authority considered a request to restore land granted to members of a protected community.
predicates.unauthorized_transfer: The land had been transferred without the required permission.
predicates.authority_acted_after_moderate_delay: The authority acted after a delay of a number of years that was not comparable to the much longer delays discussed in the cited cases.
predicates.protective_statutory_purpose: The governing law was intended to protect members of a disadvantaged community from losing granted land through exploitation.

issues.definition: In a granted-land restoration proceeding involving an unauthorized transfer, a moderate delay does not bar action when the governing law has a protective purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A contention raised for the first time at the final appellate stage may be declined when it is absent from the pleadings and contradicts the party's earlier factual position.
material_facts: The purchaser had consistently argued in the lower forums that prior permission had been obtained.
The authorities found that the purported permission documents were forged and fabricated.
Only before the Supreme Court did the purchaser argue that permission was unnecessary after the grant's non-alienation period expired.
That contention had not been pleaded in the forums below and depended on a factual situation different from the one previously asserted.
issues.conclusion: The newly raised contention could not be countenanced because it was not merely a legal plea and was inconsistent with the case previously advanced.
issues.legal_principle: A party cannot ordinarily advance at the final appellate stage a contention that was not pleaded below and that is inconsistent with its earlier factual case, particularly where the contention is raised in response to an adverse factual finding and requires a different factual basis.

predicates.final_appellate_proceeding: A party raised the contention while its case was before the final appellate court.
predicates.new_contention_not_pleaded_below: The party had not advanced the contention in its pleadings or arguments before the lower forums.
predicates.new_contention_conflicts_with_prior_fact: The new contention conflicted with the party's earlier assertion about what had happened.

issues.definition: At the final appellate stage, a contention may not be entertained when it was not raised below and conflicts with the party's earlier factual position.

issues.legal_issue: Suppression of material documents need not alone result in dismissal when the court can decide the dispute on its merits.
material_facts: The purchaser did not fully disclose documents and relied on documents said to establish prior permission.
The lower authorities had found the purported permission documents forged and fabricated, and related criminal proceedings remained pending.
The Supreme Court concluded that the merits of the dispute could be addressed without deciding the suppression objection as an independent ground for dismissal.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not dismissed solely for suppression; the court proceeded to decide the merits and upheld the orders on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: K.D. Sharma v. Steel Authority of India Ltd. states that a court may refuse to proceed where a litigant has deceived it through a misleading disclosure, and Hari Narain v. Badri Das recognizes that leave obtained by suppression does not prevent denial of relief. Here, however, the court found it unnecessary to non-suit the purchaser on suppression alone and determined the merits instead.

predicates.appellate_review: A court reviewed a dispute at the appellate stage.
predicates.material_information_was_suppressed: A party failed to fully disclose material documents or facts in presenting its case.
predicates.merits_can_resolve_the_dispute: The court could resolve the dispute by deciding the substantive legal and factual issues.

issues.definition: When a party suppresses material information but the dispute can be resolved on its merits, the court may decide those merits without dismissing the case solely for suppression.
